A(a𝟏mb𝟏n)=(bn𝟏mam𝟏n).A\binom{a\mathbf 1_m}{b\mathbf 1_n} =\binom{b\,n\,\mathbf 1_m}{a\,m\,\mathbf 1_n}.

For this to equal λ(a𝟏m,b𝟏n)\lambda(a\mathbf 1_m,b\mathbf 1_n) we need

bn=λa,am=λb.bn=\lambda a,\qquad am=\lambda b.

Eliminating: λ2=mn\lambda^2=mn, so λ=±mn\lambda=\pm\sqrt{mn}. Each gives one eigenvector. This gives two more eigenvalues.

Conclusion. The spectrum of Km,nK_{m,n} is

σ(Km,n)={mn,0m+n−2,−mn}.\boxed{\;\sigma(K_{m,n})=\{\sqrt{mn},\;0^{m+n-2},\;-\sqrt{mn}\}.\;}

In particular:

  • K1,nK_{1,n} (star), with n≥2n\ge2: eigenvalues ±n\pm\sqrt n and 00 with multiplicity n−1n-1.
  • Kn,nK_{n,n} with n≥2n\ge2: eigenvalues ±n\pm n and 00 with multiplicity 2n−22n-2.
  • Trace check: 0=mn+0+(−mn)0=\sqrt{mn}+0+(-\sqrt{mn}). tr(A2)=2mn\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=2mn.

Q75. Find the sum of entries of the adjacency matrix of a tree. If AA is the adjacency matrix of a tree, what is tr(Ak)\operatorname{tr}(A^k) for odd kk?

Sum of entries. For any graph,

∑i,jaij=𝟏TA𝟏=∑ideg(i)=2|E|.\sum_{i,j} a_{ij}=\mathbf 1^T A\mathbf 1=\sum_{i}\deg(i)=2|E|.

For a tree on nn vertices, m=n−1m=n-1, so

𝟏TA𝟏=2(n−1).\boxed{\mathbf 1^T A\mathbf 1 = 2(n-1).}

Trace of odd powers. Two equivalent arguments:

  • Combinatorial. tr(Ak)\operatorname{tr}(A^k) equals the number of closed walks of length kk in the graph. A tree is bipartite; every closed walk in a bipartite graph has even length. Hence, for odd kk,
tr(Ak)=0for every odd k.\boxed{\operatorname{tr}(A^k)=0\ \text{for every odd }k.}
  • Spectral. A tree is bipartite, so its eigenvalues are symmetric about 00: if λ\lambda is an eigenvalue, then −λ-\lambda is too, with the same multiplicity. Hence the sum of kk-th powers of eigenvalues vanishes for odd kk:
tr(Ak)=∑iλik=0(k odd).\operatorname{tr}(A^k)=\sum_i\lambda_i^k=0\qquad(k\text{ odd}).

For even k=2rk=2r, tr(A2r)=∑iλi2r≥0\operatorname{tr}(A^{2r})=\sum_i\lambda_i^{2r}\ge 0, with equality iff A=0A=0 (empty graph); in particular, a tree with n≥2n\ge 2 has tr(A2)=2(n−1)>0\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=2(n-1)>0.

Q76. Let XX be a connected bipartite graph on at least three vertices. Then XX has three distinct eigenvalues if and only if XX is a complete bipartite graph.

Solution. Let XX have at least three vertices. If X=Km,nX=K_{m,n}, then Q74 gives the three distinct eigenvalues mn,0,−mn\sqrt{mn},0,-\sqrt{mn}.

Conversely, suppose XX has three distinct adjacency eigenvalues. Bipartite spectrum symmetry gives the values −λ,0,λ-\lambda,0,\lambda, where λ>0\lambda>0. Since AA is real symmetric, its minimal polynomial is x(x−λ)(x+λ)x(x-\lambda)(x+\lambda). Thus A3=λ2AA^3=\lambda^2 A.

Suppose vertices u,vu,v in opposite parts are nonadjacent. A shortest path from uu to vv has odd length at least three. Its first four vertices give a length-three walk from uu to a vertex ww that is nonadjacent to uu, because an edge uwuw would shorten the path. Hence (A3)uw≥1(A^3)_{uw}\ge1, but Auw=0A_{uw}=0, contradicting A3=λ2AA^3=\lambda^2 A. Every pair in opposite parts is therefore adjacent.

Q77. Let TT be a tree and AA its adjacency matrix. Then AA is non-singular if and only if TT has a perfect matching.

Solution. Use the Leibniz expansion of the determinant:

detA=∑σ∈Snsign(σ)∏i=1nai,σ(i).\det A=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)\prod_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,\sigma(i)}.

Which permutations contribute? A term is nonzero iff ai,σ(i)=1a_{i,\sigma(i)}=1 for all ii, i.e. iσ(i)∈E(T)i\sigma(i)\in E(T) for every ii. Such a σ\sigma decomposes into disjoint cycles, each of which must be a cycle in TT. Since TT is acyclic, every cycle in TT has length 22 (a single edge traversed in both directions). Hence σ\sigma is a product of n2\tfrac n2 disjoint transpositions (i,j)(i,j) with ij∈E(T)ij\in E(T), i.e. σ\sigma corresponds exactly to a perfect matching of TT.

Conversely, any perfect matching M={(i1,j1),…,(in/2,jn/2)}M=\{(i_1,j_1),\dots,(i_{n/2},j_{n/2})\} of TT gives such a permutation σM=(i1j1)⋯(in/2jn/2)\sigma_M=(i_1\,j_1)\cdots(i_{n/2}\,j_{n/2}) with nonzero contribution.

Signs. Each transposition has sign −1-1, so sign(σM)=(−1)n/2\operatorname{sign}(\sigma_M)=(-1)^{n/2} is the same for every perfect matching. Therefore

detA=∑M(−1)n/2=(−1)n/2⋅#{perfect matchings of T}.\det A=\sum_{M}(-1)^{n/2}=(-1)^{n/2}\cdot\#\{\text{perfect matchings of }T\}.

Hence detA≠0\det A\neq 0 iff TT has at least one perfect matching. In particular, if nn is odd, detA=0\det A=0 automatically, as expected.

Examples.

  • Star K1,3K_{1,3}: no perfect matching, detA=0\det A=0 (indeed 00 is an eigenvalue).
  • Path P4P_4: has the unique perfect matching {12,34}\{12,34\}, and detA=(−1)2⋅1=1\det A=(-1)^2\cdot 1=1. (Indeed the eigenvalues 2cos(kπ/5)2\cos(k\pi/5) contain no zero.)
  • Path P5P_5 on 55 vertices: nn odd, so no perfect matching and detA=0\det A=0.

Q78. If GG is a tree then its adjacency matrix can be written in the form N+NTN+N^T where NN is nilpotent.

Solution. Let TT be a tree with vertex set V={1,…,n}V=\{1,\dots,n\}. Pick any vertex rr as root. Direct every edge toward rr: for each vertex v≠rv\neq r, the edge joining vv to its parent is directed v→par(v)v\to\mathrm{par}(v).

Define N∈{0,1}n×nN\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n} by

Nij={1if j=par(i),i≠r,0otherwise.N_{ij}=\begin{cases}1 & \text{if }j=\mathrm{par}(i),\; i\neq r,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

So Nij=1N_{ij}=1 iff there is a directed edge i→ji\to j.

Key identity: A=N+NTA=N+N^T. For distinct i,ji,j:

(N+NT)ij=Nij+Nji.(N+N^T)_{ij}=N_{ij}+N_{ji}.

If {i,j}∈E(T)\{i,j\}\in E(T), exactly one of i=par(j)i=\mathrm{par}(j) or j=par(i)j=\mathrm{par}(i) holds, so Nij+Nji=1=AijN_{ij}+N_{ji}=1=A_{ij}. If {i,j}∉E(T)\{i,j\}\notin E(T), neither is a parent of the other, so Nij=Nji=0=AijN_{ij}=N_{ji}=0=A_{ij}.

The diagonal entries are Nii=0N_{ii}=0 (no vertex is its own parent) and NiiT=0N^T_{ii}=0, so (N+NT)ii=0=Aii(N+N^T)_{ii}=0=A_{ii}. Hence A=N+NTA=N+N^T.

Nilpotency of NN. The (i,j)(i,j)-entry of NkN^k counts directed walks of length kk from ii to jj. Every directed edge points one level closer to the root, so a directed walk of length kk from ii must land on the kk-th ancestor of ii. If hh is the maximum depth in TT (with root at depth 00), no directed walk has length greater than hh. Hence

Nk=0for all k>h,N^k=0\quad\text{for all }k>h,

so NN is nilpotent (nilpotency index ≤h+1≤n\le h+1\le n).

Q79. Show that out of all trees, the star graph has the largest algebraic connectivity.

Solution. Recall that the algebraic connectivity of a graph GG is the second-smallest eigenvalue λ2(L(G))\lambda_2(L(G)) of its Laplacian. We use the following classical result of Fiedler.

Fiedler's theorem. For any tree TT on n≥3n\ge 3 vertices,

λ2(L(T))≤1,\lambda_2(L(T))\le 1,

with equality if and only if TT is the star K1,n−1K_{1,n-1}.

(Sketch of the mechanism: Fiedler's inequality λ2(G)≤κ(G)\lambda_2(G)\le\kappa(G) gives λ2(T)≤1\lambda_2(T)\le1 for every tree on n≥3n\ge3 vertices, since trees on n≥3n\ge3 are not complete and have vertex-connectivity 11. A finer analysis of the Fiedler vector on trees shows equality forces a single vertex to be adjacent to all others, i.e. T=K1,n−1T=K_{1,n-1}.)

Verification for the star. For K1,n−1K_{1,n-1} with centre cc and leaves ℓ1,…,ℓn−1\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{n-1}, the Laplacian has

L=(n−1−𝟏T−𝟏In−1).L = \begin{pmatrix} n-1 & -\mathbf 1^T \\ -\mathbf 1 & I_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}.

Its eigenvalues are

0,1,…,1⏟n−2times,n.0,\quad \underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{n-2\ \text{times}},\quad n.

Hence λ2(K1,n−1)=1\lambda_2(K_{1,n-1})=1.

Verification for the path. For PnP_n,

λ2(Pn)=2−2cosπn.\lambda_2(P_n)=2-2\cos\frac{\pi}{n}.

For n=3n=3 we get λ2=2−2cos(π/3)=2−1=1\lambda_2=2-2\cos(\pi/3)=2-1=1, consistent with P3=K1,2P_3=K_{1,2}. For n≥4n\ge4, cos(π/n)>cos(π/3)=12\cos(\pi/n)>\cos(\pi/3)=\tfrac12, so λ2(Pn)<1\lambda_2(P_n)<1.

Conclusion. Among all trees on n≥3n\ge3 vertices, the star achieves the maximum possible value λ2=1\lambda_2=1; every other tree has λ2<1\lambda_2<1. Thus the star maximises algebraic connectivity among trees.

Q80. Show that the algebraic connectivity of the complete bipartite graph Km,nK_{m,n}, for m+n≥3m+n\ge3, is min{m,n}\min\{m,n\}.

Solution. Let U={u1,…,um}U=\{u_1,\dots,u_m\}, V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}. Order vertices as UU then VV. The Laplacian is

L(Km,n)=(nIm−J−JTmIn),L(K_{m,n})=\begin{pmatrix} nI_m & -J \\ -J^T & mI_n \end{pmatrix},

where J=Jm×nJ=J_{m\times n}. We compute all eigenvalues.

Eigenvalue 0 (multiplicity 1). L(𝟏m,𝟏n)=0L(\mathbf 1_m,\mathbf 1_n)=0, since the row sums of LL are all zero. So 𝟏m+n\mathbf 1_{m+n} is the (unique, since Km,nK_{m,n} is connected) eigenvector for eigenvalue 00.

Eigenvalue nn (multiplicity m−1m-1). Take x∈ℝmx\in\mathbb R^m with ∑ixi=0\sum_i x_i=0 and consider (x,0)(x,0). Then

L(x0)=(nx−JTx)=(nx0),L\binom{x}{0}=\binom{nx}{-J^Tx}=\binom{nx}{0},

since JTx=(∑ixi)𝟏n=0J^Tx=(\sum_ix_i)\mathbf 1_n=0. So (x,0)(x,0) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue nn. This gives m−1m-1 independent eigenvectors.

Eigenvalue mm (multiplicity n−1n-1). Similarly, for y∈ℝny\in\mathbb R^n with ∑jyj=0\sum_j y_j=0, the vector (0,y)(0,y) satisfies L(0,y)=(0,my)L(0,y)=(0,my). This gives n−1n-1 independent eigenvectors with eigenvalue mm.

Eigenvalue m+nm+n (multiplicity 1). Consider (a𝟏m,b𝟏n)(a\mathbf 1_m, b\mathbf 1_n). Using J𝟏n=n𝟏mJ\mathbf 1_n=n\mathbf 1_m and JT𝟏m=m𝟏nJ^T\mathbf 1_m=m\mathbf 1_n,

L(a𝟏mb𝟏n)=(an𝟏m−bn𝟏m−am𝟏n+bm𝟏n)=(n(a−b)𝟏mm(b−a)𝟏n).L\binom{a\mathbf 1_m}{b\mathbf 1_n}=\binom{an\mathbf 1_m-bn\mathbf 1_m}{-am\mathbf 1_n+bm\mathbf 1_n} =\binom{n(a-b)\mathbf 1_m}{m(b-a)\mathbf 1_n}.

For this to equal λ(a𝟏m,b𝟏n)\lambda(a\mathbf 1_m,b\mathbf 1_n):

n(a−b)=λa,m(b−a)=λb.n(a-b)=\lambda a,\qquad m(b-a)=\lambda b.

For (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b)\neq(0,0) with a≠ba\ne b (the a=ba=b case gives eigenvalue 00), divide the two equations: n(a−b)m(b−a)=ab\dfrac{n(a-b)}{m(b-a)}=\dfrac{a}{b}, i.e. −nm=ab-\dfrac nm=\dfrac ab. Setting a=−na=-n, b=mb=m gives

λ=n(a−b)/a=n(−n−m)/(−n)=m+n.\lambda=n(a-b)/a = n(-n-m)/(-n)=m+n.

So (a,b)=(−n,m)(a,b)=(-n,m) gives eigenvalue m+nm+n.

Total count. 1+(m−1)+(n−1)+1=m+n1+(m-1)+(n-1)+1=m+n eigenvectors, so we have all eigenvalues:

σ(L(Km,n))={0,n(m−1),m(n−1),m+n}.\boxed{\sigma(L(K_{m,n}))=\{0,\; n^{(m-1)},\; m^{(n-1)},\; m+n\}.}

Conclusion. The second-smallest eigenvalue is

λ2(Km,n)=min{n,m}=min{m,n}.\lambda_2(K_{m,n})=\min\{n,\,m\}=\min\{m,n\}.

(When m=1m=1 or n=1n=1: the eigenvalue nn or mm with multiplicity 00 is absent, but the remaining set still gives λ2=min{m,n}=1\lambda_2=\min\{m,n\}=1.)

For the exceptional graph K1,1=K2K_{1,1}=K_2, the Laplacian eigenvalues are 0,20,2, so λ2=2\lambda_2=2.

Checks.

  • Trace: 0+n(m−1)+m(n−1)+(m+n)=2mn=2|E(Km,n)|0+n(m-1)+m(n-1)+(m+n)=2mn=2|E(K_{m,n})|. ✓
  • Kn,nK_{n,n} with n≥2n\ge2: eigenvalues 0,n(n−1),n(n−1),2n0,n^{(n-1)},n^{(n-1)},2n, so λ2=n\lambda_2=n. ✓
  • K1,nK_{1,n} (star), with n≥2n\ge2: m=1m=1, eigenvalues 0,1(n−1),n+10,1^{(n-1)},n+1, so λ2=1\lambda_2=1. ✓ (Consistent with Q79.)

Graphs with a nice minimal polynomial

Q81. Prove that for the complete bipartite graph Km,nK_{m,n} one has A3=mnAA^3=mn\,A. Deduce its minimal polynomial.

Proof by counting walks. Let the parts be UU (|U|=m|U|=m) and VV (|V|=n|V|=n). By Q9, (A3)ij(A^3)_{ij} is the number of walks i→a→b→ji\to a\to b\to j of length 33. We must show it equals mnAijmn\,A_{ij}.

  • ii and jj in different parts (say i∈Ui\in U, j∈Vj\in V; then Aij=1A_{ij}=1). Choose aa to be any vertex of VV (nn ways) and bb to be any vertex of UU (mm ways). Then i∼ai\sim a, a∼ba\sim b, b∼jb\sim j always hold, and every walk has this form. So (A3)ij=mn(A^3)_{ij}=mn.
  • ii and jj in the same part (so Aij=0A_{ij}=0). Each step of a walk switches parts, so after 33 steps (an odd number) the walk ends in the other part. Hence there is no such walk and (A3)ij=0(A^3)_{ij}=0.

Both cases give (A3)ij=mnAij(A^3)_{ij}=mn\,A_{ij}, i.e. A3=mnAA^3=mn\,A. ▫\square

Matrix proof (check). With A=(0Jm×nJn×m0)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&J_{m\times n}\\ J_{n\times m}&0\end{pmatrix}, using Jm×nJn×m=nJmJ_{m\times n}J_{n\times m}=nJ_m and Jn×mJm×n=mJnJ_{n\times m}J_{m\times n}=mJ_n,

A2=(nJm00mJn),A3=A⋅A2=(0mnJm×nmnJn×m0)=mnA.A^2=\begin{pmatrix}nJ_m&0\\0&mJ_n\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^3=A\cdot A^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&mn\,J_{m\times n}\\ mn\,J_{n\times m}&0\end{pmatrix}=mn\,A.

Minimal polynomial. AA satisfies x3−mnx=x(x−mn)(x+mn)x^3-mn\,x=x(x-\sqrt{mn})(x+\sqrt{mn}). By Q74 the eigenvalues are ±mn\pm\sqrt{mn} and 00 (the eigenvalue 00 occurs when m+n>2m+n>2). So by Q1, for (m,n)≠(1,1)(m,n)\ne(1,1),

mA(x)=x3−mnx=x(x2−mn).\boxed{\,m_A(x)=x^3-mn\,x=x\,(x^2-mn).\,}

For K1,1=K2K_{1,1}=K_2 one has A2=IA^2=I and mA(x)=x2−1m_A(x)=x^2-1.

This is the converse direction of Q76: a connected bipartite graph with three distinct eigenvalues is complete bipartite, and then AA satisfies the cubic x3=mnxx^3=mn\,x.

Q82. What is a complete multipartite graph? How does it differ from a complete bipartite graph? Draw examples and give the adjacency matrix.

Definition. Partition the vertex set into t≥2t\ge2 non-empty parts V1,…,VtV_1,\dots,V_t with |Vi|=ni|V_i|=n_i. The complete multipartite graph Kn1,n2,…,ntK_{n_1,n_2,\dots,n_t} has

u∼v⇔u and v lie in different parts.u\sim v\iff u\text{ and }v\text{ lie in different parts}.

So vertices in the same part are never adjacent, and every vertex is adjacent to all vertices outside its own part. For t=2t=2 this is Km,nK_{m,n}. If all ni=1n_i=1 we get KtK_t (the complete graph, which is excluded from this section).

Vertices of the same colour form one part. In K1,2,2K_{1,2,2} the two red vertices are not adjacent (they are opposite corners of the square), the two blue ones are not adjacent, and the green vertex in the middle is adjacent to all four others. This graph is the wheel with 44 spokes.

Adjacency matrix. Order the vertices part by part. Then

A=J−diag(Jn1,…,Jnt),A=J-\operatorname{diag}(J_{n_1},\dots,J_{n_t}),

i.e. all blocks are all-ones blocks except the diagonal blocks, which are zero. For t=2t=2 this is the familiar A=(0Jm×nJn×m0)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&J_{m\times n}\\J_{n\times m}&0\end{pmatrix} of Km,nK_{m,n}.

Differences between Km,nK_{m,n} and Kn1,…,ntK_{n_1,\dots,n_t} with t≥3t\ge3.

  • Odd cycles. Km,nK_{m,n} is bipartite: it has no odd cycle and no triangle. If t≥3t\ge3, pick one vertex from each of three parts; they form a triangle. Hence a complete multipartite graph with t≥3t\ge3 parts is not bipartite.
  • Spectrum. The spectrum of Km,nK_{m,n} is symmetric about 00 (Q13): {±mn,0,…}\{\pm\sqrt{mn},0,\dots\}. For t≥3t\ge3 it is not symmetric. For example K2,2,2K_{2,2,2} has spectrum {4,03,(−2)2}\{4,0^3,(-2)^2\} (Q83).
  • Number of distinct eigenvalues. If all parts have the same size s≥2s\ge2, both Ks,sK_{s,s} and Kt×sK_{t\times s} (t≥3t\ge3) have exactly 33 distinct eigenvalues (Q81, Q86), but with different shapes: {s,0,−s}\{s,0,-s\} versus {(t−1)s,0,−s}\{(t-1)s,0,-s\}.
  • Complement. The complement of Km,nK_{m,n} is Km∪KnK_m\cup K_n. The complement of Kn1,…,ntK_{n_1,\dots,n_t} is Kn1∪⋯∪KntK_{n_1}\cup\cdots\cup K_{n_t}, a disjoint union of cliques.

Characterization. GG is complete multipartite ⇔\iff "equal or non-adjacent" is an equivalence relation ⇔\iff G¯\overline G is a disjoint union of complete graphs ⇔\iff GG has no induced subgraph on three vertices with exactly one edge (that is, u≁vu\not\sim v, v≁wv\not\sim w forces u≁wu\not\sim w).

Counting the edges. Let nin_i be the number of vertices in part ViV_i, and let n=n1+⋯+ntn=n_1+\cdots+n_t be the total number of vertices. For each pair of distinct parts Vi,VjV_i,V_j, every vertex in one part is joined to every vertex in the other, giving ninjn_i n_j edges. Count each pair of parts once:

|E|=∑1≤i<j≤tninj=n2−(n12+⋯+nt2)2.|E|=\sum_{1\le i<j\le t} n_i n_j =\frac{n^2-(n_1^2+\cdots+n_t^2)}{2}.

The second equality follows by expanding (n1+⋯+nt)2(n_1+\cdots+n_t)^2: the square terms are ni2n_i^2, and each cross term ninjn_i n_j occurs twice.

Example. In K1,2,2K_{1,2,2}, the three pairs of parts contribute 1⋅21\cdot2, 1⋅21\cdot2, and 2⋅22\cdot2 edges, for a total of 88.

The three-eigenvalue formulas in the next questions need equal part sizes. For unequal sizes the degrees differ, the graph is not regular, and the spectrum is much less tidy.

Q83. Study K2,2,2K_{2,2,2} (the octahedron): draw it, find A2A^2, the minimal polynomial and the spectrum.

The graph. Three parts {a,a′},{b,b′},{c,c′}\{a,a'\},\{b,b'\},\{c,c'\}. It has 66 vertices, is 44-regular, and has 1212 edges: it is K6K_6 minus a perfect matching, the 11-skeleton of the octahedron. In the picture the non-adjacent pairs are the three antipodal pairs of the hexagon.

Step 1: A2A^2 by common neighbours (Q9).

  • Diagonal: (A2)ii=4(A^2)_{ii}=4.
  • Non-adjacent pair (same colour, e.g. a,a′a,a'): common neighbours are all 44 other vertices, so the entry is 44.
  • Adjacent pair (e.g. a,ba,b): common neighbours are the vertices outside {a,a′,b,b′}\{a,a',b,b'\}, namely c,c′c,c', so the entry is 22.

Let M=J−I−AM=J-I-A be the matching matrix (11 exactly for the pairs aa′,bb′,cc′aa',bb',cc'). Then A2=4I+2A+4M=4I+2A+4(J−I−A)A^2=4I+2A+4M=4I+2A+4(J-I-A), i.e.

A2+2A=4J.A^2+2A=4J.

Step 2: minimal polynomial. Since AJ=4JAJ=4J, multiplying by A−4IA-4I gives A(A+2I)(A−4I)=0A(A+2I)(A-4I)=0. The graph is connected with diameter 22, so by Q53 it has at least three distinct eigenvalues. Therefore

mA(x)=x(x+2)(x−4).m_A(x)=x(x+2)(x-4).

Step 3: eigenvectors, directly. Write A=J−diag(J2,J2,J2)A=J-\operatorname{diag}(J_2,J_2,J_2).

  • x=(1,−1,0,0,0,0)x=(1,-1,0,0,0,0) (and similarly on the other two parts): Jx=0Jx=0 and diag(J2,J2,J2)x=0\operatorname{diag}(J_2,J_2,J_2)x=0, so Ax=0Ax=0. This gives 33 independent eigenvectors for 00.
  • x=(α,α,β,β,γ,γ)x=(\alpha,\alpha,\beta,\beta,\gamma,\gamma) with α+β+γ=0\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0: Jx=0Jx=0, and diag(J2,J2,J2)x=2x\operatorname{diag}(J_2,J_2,J_2)x=2x, so Ax=−2xAx=-2x. This gives a 22-dimensional eigenspace for −2-2.
  • x=𝐞x=\mathbf e: A𝐞=4𝐞A\mathbf e=4\mathbf e.

1+3+2=61+3+2=6, so we have found all eigenvalues:

σ(K2,2,2)={4,0(3),(−2)(2)}.\boxed{\sigma(K_{2,2,2})=\{4,\;0^{(3)},\;(-2)^{(2)}\}.}

Checks. trA=4−4=0\operatorname{tr}A=4-4=0. trA2=16+2⋅4=24=2|E|\operatorname{tr}A^2=16+2\cdot4=24=2|E|. trA3=64+2(−8)=48=6×#triangles\operatorname{tr}A^3=64+2(-8)=48=6\times\#\text{triangles}, so there are 88 triangles (the 88 faces of the octahedron, one vertex from each part). J=14(A2+2A)J=\tfrac14(A^2+2A) is a polynomial in AA, as in Q56.

Q84. Let G=K2,2,…,2G=K_{2,2,\dots,2} with nn parts of size 22 (the cocktail-party graph, K2nK_{2n} minus a perfect matching). Find the spectrum and the minimal polynomial.

Picture. Think of KnK_n and replace each vertex by a pair of non-adjacent vertices; two vertices are adjacent iff they come from different vertices of KnK_n. The figure shows n=4n=4; each thick line means "all four edges between the two pairs".

Matrix form. GG has 2n2n vertices and is (2n−2)(2n-2)-regular. Let MM be the permutation matrix of the perfect matching that pairs each vertex with its twin (M2=IM^2=I, MJ=JM=JMJ=JM=J). Then

A=J−I−M.A=J-I-M.

Eigenvalues. The involution MM has eigenvalues ±1\pm1:

  • M𝐞=𝐞M\mathbf e=\mathbf e: A𝐞=(2n)𝐞−𝐞−𝐞=(2n−2)𝐞A\mathbf e=(2n)\mathbf e-\mathbf e-\mathbf e=(2n-2)\mathbf e.
  • x⊥𝐞x\perp\mathbf e with Mx=xMx=x (equal on twins, sum zero): Ax=0−x−x=−2xAx=0-x-x=-2x. The space of vectors equal on twins has dimension nn; removing 𝐞\mathbf e leaves dimension n−1n-1.
  • xx with Mx=−xMx=-x (opposite on twins): automatically x⊥𝐞x\perp\mathbf e, so Ax=0−x+x=0Ax=0-x+x=0. This space has dimension nn.

Total 1+(n−1)+n=2n1+(n-1)+n=2n, so

σ={2n−2,0(n),(−2)(n−1)},mA(x)=x(x+2)(x−(2n−2)).\boxed{\sigma=\{2n-2,\;0^{(n)},\;(-2)^{(n-1)}\},\qquad m_A(x)=x\,(x+2)\,(x-(2n-2)).}

(Here n≥2n\ge2; for n=1n=1 the graph is two isolated vertices.)

Graph-theoretic check. Adjacent vertices have 2n−42n-4 common neighbours, twins have 2n−22n-2, and so A2=(2n−2)I+(2n−4)A+(2n−2)MA^2=(2n-2)I+(2n-4)A+(2n-2)M. Substituting M=J−I−AM=J-I-A gives A2+2A=(2n−2)JA^2+2A=(2n-2)J.

Small cases.

  • n=2n=2: K2,2=C4K_{2,2}=C_4, spectrum {2,02,−2}\{2,0^2,-2\}.
  • n=3n=3: octahedron K2,2,2K_{2,2,2}, spectrum {4,03,(−2)2}\{4,0^3,(-2)^2\} (Q83).
  • n=4n=4: K2,2,2,2K_{2,2,2,2}, 66-regular on 88 vertices, spectrum {6,04,(−2)3}\{6,0^4,(-2)^3\}.

Q85. Study Kt,t,tK_{t,t,t} (three parts of size tt): find A2A^2, the spectrum and the minimal polynomial. What happens for t=1t=1 and t=2t=2?

The graph. It has 3t3t vertices and is 2t2t-regular. It is a blow-up of the triangle: each vertex of K3K_3 is replaced by tt non-adjacent vertices.

Matrix form. A=J3t−diag(Jt,Jt,Jt)A=J_{3t}-\operatorname{diag}(J_t,J_t,J_t).

Eigenvalues.

  • Sum zero inside each part. If xx is supported on one part and its entries add up to 00, then Jx=0Jx=0 and Jtx=0J_tx=0, so Ax=0Ax=0. Each part gives a space of dimension t−1t-1, so 00 has multiplicity ≥3(t−1)\ge3(t-1).

Q86. For the complete multipartite graph Kt×sK_{t\times s} (t≥2t\ge2 parts, each of size s≥2s\ge2), show that A2+sA=(t−1)sJA^2+sA=(t-1)s\,J, and deduce that the minimal polynomial of AA is x(x+s)(x−(t−1)s)x\,(x+s)\,(x-(t-1)s).

Setup. GG has tsts vertices; two vertices are adjacent iff they lie in different parts. So GG is kk-regular with k=(t−1)sk=(t-1)s. Let P=J−I−AP=J-I-A be the adjacency matrix of "distinct vertices in the same part" (a disjoint union of tt copies of KsK_s).

This question contains Q81 (t=2t=2, Ks,sK_{s,s}), Q84 (s=2s=2), Q83 (t=3,s=2t=3,s=2) and Q85 (t=3t=3) as special cases.

Step 1: count common neighbours. By Q9, (A2)ij(A^2)_{ij} is the number of common neighbours of ii and jj (and degi\deg i if i=ji=j).

  • i=ji=j: (A2)ii=k=(t−1)s(A^2)_{ii}=k=(t-1)s.
  • i≠ji\ne j in the same part (non-adjacent): a common neighbour is any vertex outside that part, giving (t−1)s(t-1)s of them.
  • i,ji,j in different parts (adjacent): a common neighbour is any vertex outside both parts, giving (t−2)s(t-2)s.

Therefore

A2=(t−1)sI+(t−2)sA+(t−1)sP.A^2=(t-1)s\,I+(t-2)s\,A+(t-1)s\,P.

Step 2: eliminate PP. Substituting P=J−I−AP=J-I-A,

A2=(t−1)sI+(t−2)sA+(t−1)s(J−I−A)=(t−1)sJ−sA,A^2=(t-1)s\,I+(t-2)s\,A+(t-1)s\,(J-I-A)=(t-1)s\,J-s\,A,

that is,

A2+sA=kJ,k=(t−1)s.A^2+sA=kJ,\qquad k=(t-1)s.

Step 3: the polynomial. GG is regular, so AJ=kJAJ=kJ (Q54(a)). Multiply the identity by A−kIA-kI:

(A−kI)A(A+sI)=k(A−kI)J=k(kJ−kJ)=0.(A-kI)\,A\,(A+sI)=k\,(A-kI)J=k\,(kJ-kJ)=0.

So mA(x)m_A(x) divides x(x+s)(x−k)x\,(x+s)(x-k). Conversely, GG is connected and not complete (s≥2s\ge2 gives non-adjacent vertices, and t≥2t\ge2 gives diameter 22), so by Q53, AA has at least 33 distinct eigenvalues. Hence all three k,0,−sk,0,-s occur, and

mA(x)=x(x+s)(x−(t−1)s).\boxed{\,m_A(x)=x\,(x+s)\,(x-(t-1)s).\,}

Multiplicities. kk is simple (Q54(b)). Let bb be the multiplicity of −s-s, and aa that of 00. From trA=0\operatorname{tr}A=0: k−sb=0k-sb=0, so b=t−1b=t-1. From 1+a+b=ts1+a+b=ts: a=t(s−1)a=t(s-1). Hence

σ(Kt×s)={(t−1)s,0t(s−1),(−s)t−1}.\sigma(K_{t\times s})=\{(t-1)s,\;0^{\,t(s-1)},\;(-s)^{\,t-1}\}.

Second proof (quotient idea). Vectors with zero sum inside every part are killed by AA: this gives t(s−1)t(s-1) eigenvectors for 00. On vectors constant on each part, AA acts like the t×tt\times t matrix s(Jt−It)s\,(J_t-I_t), whose eigenvalues are (t−1)s(t-1)s (once) and −s-s (t−1t-1 times). The counts add up to tsts.

Special cases.

  • t=2t=2: Ks,sK_{s,s}, k=sk=s, A2+sA=sJA^2+sA=sJ, spectrum {s,0(2s−2),−s}\{s,\;0^{(2s-2)},\;-s\}. Multiplying A2+sA=sJA^2+sA=sJ by AA and using AJ=sJAJ=sJ recovers A3=s2AA^3=s^2A (Q81).
  • s=2s=2: cocktail-party graph (Q84).
  • t=3t=3: Ks,s,sK_{s,s,s} (Q85).

Q87. A kk-regular graph on vv vertices is strongly regular with parameters (v,k,λ,μ)(v,k,\lambda,\mu) if adjacent vertices have exactly λ\lambda common neighbours and non-adjacent distinct vertices have exactly μ\mu. Show that A2=kI+λA+μ(J−I−A)A^2=kI+\lambda A+\mu(J-I-A), and deduce that a connected strongly regular graph has at most three distinct eigenvalues. Find the minimal polynomials of C5C_5 and the Petersen graph.

Step 1: the matrix equation. By Q9, (A2)ij(A^2)_{ij} counts common neighbours (and equals degi=k\deg i=k for i=ji=j). It is kk on the diagonal, λ\lambda where Aij=1A_{ij}=1, and μ\mu where i≠ji\ne j and Aij=0A_{ij}=0, i.e. where (J−I−A)ij=1(J-I-A)_{ij}=1. Hence

A2=kI+λA+μ(J−I−A),i.e.A2−(λ−μ)A−(k−μ)I=μJ.A^2=kI+\lambda A+\mu\,(J-I-A),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad A^2-(\lambda-\mu)A-(k-\mu)I=\mu J.

Step 2: eigenvalues. Let Ax=θxAx=\theta x with x⊥𝐞x\perp\mathbf e. Then Jx=0Jx=0, so

θ2−(λ−μ)θ−(k−μ)=0.\theta^2-(\lambda-\mu)\theta-(k-\mu)=0.

This quadratic has at most two roots. Together with θ=k\theta=k (eigenvector 𝐞\mathbf e), AA has at most three distinct eigenvalues. Equivalently, multiplying the identity of Step 1 by A−kIA-kI kills JJ (since AJ=kJAJ=kJ):

(A−kI)(A2−(λ−μ)A−(k−μ)I)=0.(A-kI)(A^2-(\lambda-\mu)A-(k-\mu)I)=0.

For a connected strongly regular graph that is not complete, this is the minimal polynomial (three distinct eigenvalues by Q53, since diam=2\operatorname{diam}=2).

Example 1: C5C_5, parameters (5,2,0,1)(5,2,0,1). Adjacent vertices of C5C_5 have no common neighbour (λ=0\lambda=0); non-adjacent vertices have exactly one (μ=1\mu=1). So

A2+A−I=J,mA(x)=(x−2)(x2+x−1),σ={2,(−1+52)(2),(−1−52)(2)}.A^2+A-I=J,\qquad m_A(x)=(x-2)(x^2+x-1),\qquad \sigma=\{2,\ (\tfrac{-1+\sqrt5}{2})^{(2)},\ (\tfrac{-1-\sqrt5}{2})^{(2)}\}.

Example 2: the Petersen graph, parameters (10,3,0,1)(10,3,0,1). Take the vertices to be the 22-subsets of {1,…,5}\{1,\dots,5\}, adjacent iff disjoint. Then:

  • {a,b}∼{c,d}\{a,b\}\sim\{c,d\}: the neighbours of {a,b}\{a,b\} are the 22-subsets of {c,d,e}\{c,d,e\} and those of {c,d}\{c,d\} are the 22-subsets of {a,b,e}\{a,b,e\}; no common one, so λ=0\lambda=0.
  • {a,b}≁{a,c}\{a,b\}\not\sim\{a,c\}: the neighbours are 22-subsets of {c,d,e}\{c,d,e\} and of {b,d,e}\{b,d,e\}; the only common one is {d,e}\{d,e\}, so μ=1\mu=1.

Hence A2+A−2I=JA^2+A-2I=J, and since x2+x−2=(x−1)(x+2)x^2+x-2=(x-1)(x+2),

mA(x)=(x−3)(x−1)(x+2).\boxed{\,m_A(x)=(x-3)(x-1)(x+2).\,}

Multiplicities: with aa for 11 and bb for −2-2, a+b=9a+b=9 and trA=0\operatorname{tr}A=0 gives 3+a−2b=03+a-2b=0, so a=5a=5, b=4b=4: σ={3,1(5),(−2)(4)}\sigma=\{3,\ 1^{(5)},\ (-2)^{(4)}\}.

Summary of "nice" minimal polynomials obtained by counting walks or common neighbours: Km,nK_{m,n} (Q81): x(x2−mn)x(x^2-mn); Kt×sK_{t\times s} (Q82–Q86): x(x+s)(x−(t−1)s)x(x+s)(x-(t-1)s); C5C_5: (x−2)(x2+x−1)(x-2)(x^2+x-1); Petersen: (x−3)(x−1)(x+2)(x-3)(x-1)(x+2). For KnK_n it is (x−(n−1))(x+1)(x-(n-1))(x+1). In each connected regular case JJ is a polynomial in AA of degree (number of distinct eigenvalues) −1-1, as predicted by Q55–Q56.

Result 1 Handshaking Lemma

Theorem (Handshaking Lemma)

For every finite graph G=(V,E)G = (V, E),

∑v∈Vdeg(v)=2|E|.\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) \;=\; 2\,|E|.

Proof (Double Counting Incidences)

Consider the set of ordered pairs representing vertex-edge incidences:

S={(v,e)∈V×E:v is an endpoint of e}.S = \{(v, e) \in V \times E : v \text{ is an endpoint of } e\}.

We count |S||S| in two ways:

  1. By Vertices: A vertex vv appears in exactly deg(v)\deg(v) pairs, hence |S|=∑v∈Vdeg(v)|S| = \sum_{v \in V} \deg(v).
  2. By Edges: An edge e={x,y}e = \{x, y\} gives exactly two pairs, (x,e)(x, e) and (y,e)(y, e), hence |S|=2|E||S| = 2\,|E|.

Equating both counts gives ∑v∈Vdeg(v)=2|E|\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2\,|E|.

▫\square
degA=3,degB=2,degC=3,degD=2\deg A = 3, \deg B = 2, \deg C = 3, \deg D = 2; sum =10=2⋅5= 10 = 2 \cdot 5.

Result 2 Parity of Odd-Degree Vertices

Corollary

The number of vertices of odd degree in any finite graph is even.

Proof

Split the handshaking sum into even-degree and odd-degree vertices:

∑v∈Vdeg(v)=∑deg evendeg(v)⏟even+∑deg odddeg(v)⏟≡|Vodd|(mod2).\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{\deg\text{ even}} \deg(v)}_{\text{even}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{\deg\text{ odd}} \deg(v)}_{\equiv\, |V_{\text{odd}}| \pmod 2}.

Reducing modulo 22:

0≡∑v∈Vdeg(v)≡|Vodd|(mod2).0 \;\equiv\; \sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) \;\equiv\; |V_{\text{odd}}| \pmod 2.

Hence |Vodd||V_{\text{odd}}| is even.

▫\square
Odd-degree vertices (red): AA and CC (|Vodd|=2\vert{}V_{\text{odd}}\vert{} = 2).

Result 3 Maximum Edges in a Bipartite Graph

Theorem (Bipartite Edge Maximum)

If GG is a simple bipartite graph on nn vertices, then

|E(G)|≤⌊n24⌋.|E(G)| \;\le\; \left\lfloor \frac{n^{2}}{4} \right\rfloor.

Proof

Setup: Let V=A∪BV = A \cup B with |A|=t|A| = t and |B|=n−t|B| = n - t. Since GG is bipartite, no edges lie inside AA or inside BB, hence |E(G)|≤|A|⋅|B|=t(n−t)|E(G)| \le |A| \cdot |B| = t(n - t).

Maximise Quadratic: Define f(t)=t(n−t)=n24−(t−n2)2f(t) = t(n - t) = \frac{n^2}{4} - \left(t - \frac{n}{2}\right)^2. This is a downward parabola with vertex at t=n/2t = n/2. Over integers 0≤t≤n0 \le t \le n:

max0≤t≤nf(t)=f(⌊n2⌋)=⌊n24⌋.\max_{0 \le t \le n} f(t) \;=\; f\left(\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \right\rfloor\right) \;=\; \left\lfloor \frac{n^2}{4} \right\rfloor.

Attainment: The complete bipartite graph K⌊n/2⌋,⌈n/2⌉K_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor, \lceil n/2 \rceil} achieves equality.

▫\square
K3,3K_{3,3}: n=6n = 6, edges =9=⌊36/4⌋= 9 = \lfloor 36/4 \rfloor.

Result 4 Bipartite Characterisation (⇒\Rightarrow)

Theorem (Bipartite Characterisation)

A graph GG is bipartite if and only if GG contains no cycle of odd length.

Proof (⇒\Rightarrow: Bipartite implies no odd cycle)

Let GG be bipartite with parts A,BA, B. Take any cycle v1v2…vkv1v_1 v_2 \dots v_k v_1. Each edge joins AA to BB, so vertex colors alternate along the cycle:

v1∈A,v2∈B,v3∈A,v4∈B,…v_1 \in A,\quad v_2 \in B,\quad v_3 \in A,\quad v_4 \in B, \quad \dots

Odd-indexed vertices lie in AA, even-indexed vertices lie in BB. Since vkv_k is adjacent to v1∈Av_1 \in A, vkv_k must belong to BB, which requires kk to be even. Hence, every cycle in GG has even length.

▫\square
C5C_5 (odd, non-bipartite) vs C6C_6 (even, bipartite).

Result 5 Bipartite Characterisation (⇐\Leftarrow)

Proof (⇐\Leftarrow: No odd cycle implies Bipartite) — Detailed Breakdown

Assume every cycle of GG has even length. It suffices to treat one connected component (then union over components).

Fix a vertex vv in that component and define two sets based on shortest-path distance d(v,x)d(v, x):

V1={x∈V:d(v,x) is even},V2={x∈V:d(v,x) is odd}.V_1 = \{x \in V : d(v, x) \text{ is even}\}, \qquad V_2 = \{x \in V : d(v, x) \text{ is odd}\}.

Clearly V1∪V2=VV_1 \cup V_2 = V and V1∩V2=∅V_1 \cap V_2 = \emptyset.

Claim: No two vertices of V1V_1 are adjacent.

Use of Hypothesis: Suppose x,y∈V1x, y \in V_1 with xy∈Exy \in E. Let PxP_x and PyP_y be shortest vv-xx and vv-yy paths. Both paths have even length (by definition of V1V_1).

Then the closed walk W=Px+xy+reverse(Py)W = P_x + xy + \text{reverse}(P_y) has length:

length(W)=even+1+even=odd.\text{length}(W) = \text{even} + 1 + \text{even} = \text{odd}.

A closed odd walk always contains an odd cycle (splitting the walk at any repeated vertex leaves at least one piece of odd length). But our hypothesis states that GG contains no odd cycles — a contradiction!

Hence, no two vertices of V1V_1 are adjacent. By identical reasoning, no two vertices of V2V_2 are adjacent. Therefore, every edge joins V1V_1 to V2V_2, proving (V1,V2)(V_1, V_2) is a valid bipartition.

▫\square
Edge inside V1V_1 creates an odd closed walk, forcing an odd cycle.

Result 6 Eulerian Circuit Condition

Theorem (Eulerian Criterion)

A connected graph has a closed trail using every edge exactly once (an Eulerian circuit) iff every vertex has even degree.

Proof (Necessity & Sufficiency)

(⇒)(\Rightarrow) Necessity: Let CC be an Eulerian circuit. Each pass through v≠rv \neq r enters by one edge and leaves by another. The initial departure and final return at base vertex rr pair up as well. Thus deg(v)=2⋅(visits)\deg(v) = 2 \cdot (\text{visits}), which is even.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow) Sufficiency (Hierholzer's Algorithm):

  1. Greedy Trail: Start at any vertex and follow unused edges. Since every degree is even, the walk can only terminate by returning to the start, giving closed trail CC.
  2. Splice: If unused edges remain, connectivity gives a vertex uu of CC incident to an unused edge. Every vertex has even unused degree because the closed trail CC used an even number of edges at each vertex. Starting at uu, follow unused edges until forced to stop. The same parity argument gives a closed trail C′C^\prime at uu. Insert it into CC at uu.
  3. Iterate: Repeat until all edges are traversed.
▫\square
Figure-eight: deg(v)=4\deg(v) = 4, all other degrees =2= 2.

Hamiltonian Graphs Ore's Theorem & Dirac's Corollary

Theorem (Ore, 1960)

Let G=(V,E)G = (V, E) be a simple graph on n≥3n \ge 3 vertices. If

deg(u)+deg(v)≥n\deg(u) + \deg(v) \;\ge\; n

for every pair of non-adjacent vertices u,v∈Vu, v \in V, then GG contains a Hamiltonian cycle.

Elaborated Proof of Ore's Theorem
  1. 1. Extremal Setup: Suppose GG satisfies Ore's condition but is non-Hamiltonian. Choose GG to be edge-maximal with respect to this property.
  2. 2. Add Missing Edge & Extract Path: For non-adjacent u,v∈Vu, v \in V, adding uvuv creates a Hamiltonian cycle in G+uvG + uv. Deleting uvuv leaves a Hamiltonian path v1,v2,…,vnv_1, v_2, \dots, v_n in GG with v1=u,vn=vv_1 = u, v_n = v (v1≁vnv_1 \nsim v_n).
  3. 3. Crossing Edge Exclusion: Set S={i:v1∼vi}S = \{i : v_1 \sim v_i\} with |S|=deg(v1)|S| = \deg(v_1). If v1∼viv_1 \sim v_i, then vn≁vi−1v_n \nsim v_{i-1}; otherwise, the sequence v1→vi→vi+1…→vn→vi−1→…→v1v_1 \to v_i \to v_{i+1} \dots \to v_n \to v_{i-1} \to \dots \to v_1 forms a Hamiltonian cycle in GG, a contradiction!
  4. 4. Counting Contradiction: For each neighbor viv_i of v1v_1, vi−1v_{i-1} is a non-neighbor of vnv_n. Including v1v_1 itself, vnv_n has at least deg(v1)+1\deg(v_1) + 1 non-neighbors. Thus deg(vn)≤(n−1)−(deg(v1)+1)⟹deg(v1)+deg(vn)≤n−2\deg(v_n) \le (n - 1) - (\deg(v_1) + 1) \implies \deg(v_1) + \deg(v_n) \le n - 2, contradicting deg(v1)+deg(vn)≥n\deg(v_1) + \deg(v_n) \ge n.
▫\square
Hamiltonian path with non-adjacent v1,vnv_1, v_n. Crossing edges v1viv_1 v_i and vi−1vnv_{i-1} v_n (red) would close a Hamiltonian cycle.
Corollary (Dirac, 1952)

Let G=(V,E)G = (V, E) be a simple graph on n≥3n \ge 3 vertices. If deg(v)≥n/2\deg(v) \ge n/2 for every vertex v∈Vv \in V, then GG contains a Hamiltonian cycle.

Proof (As a Direct Corollary to Ore's Theorem)
  1. 1. Apply Dirac's Hypothesis: Let u,v∈Vu, v \in V be any pair of non-adjacent vertices in GG. By Dirac's condition:

    deg(u)≥n2anddeg(v)≥n2.\deg(u) \;\ge\; \frac{n}{2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \deg(v) \;\ge\; \frac{n}{2}.

  2. 2. Sum the Degrees: Adding both bounds yields:

    deg(u)+deg(v)≥n2+n2=n.\deg(u) + \deg(v) \;\ge\; \frac{n}{2} + \frac{n}{2} \;=\; n.

  3. 3. Conclusion via Ore's Theorem: Since deg(u)+deg(v)≥n\deg(u) + \deg(v) \ge n holds for every non-adjacent pair, Ore's condition is satisfied. By Ore's Theorem, GG contains a Hamiltonian cycle.
▫\square
Remark on Sharpness

The bound n/2n/2 is sharp: For even nn, the disjoint union Kn/2∪Kn/2K_{n/2} \cup K_{n/2} has minimum degree n2−1\frac{n}{2} - 1 and is disconnected / non-Hamiltonian.

3-regular graph (n=6,deg(v)≥3=6/2n = 6, \deg(v) \ge 3 = 6/2), guaranteeing a Hamiltonian cycle via Dirac & Ore conditions.

Result 8 Euler's Planar Formula (v−e+f=2v - e + f = 2)

Theorem (Euler's Planar Formula)

For a connected plane graph with vv vertices, ee edges, and ff faces,

v−e+f=2.v - e + f \;=\; 2.

Proof (Induction on Edges)

Base Case (GG is a tree): e=v−1e = v - 1 and f=1f = 1 (only the outer unbounded face exists). Thus v−e+f=v−(v−1)+1=2v - e + f = v - (v - 1) + 1 = 2.

Inductive Step: Suppose GG contains a cycle and pick edge e0e_0 on it.

  • Removing e0e_0 leaves G−e0G - e_0 connected (detour exists along cycle).
  • The cycle separates the plane into an inside and an outside, so the two sides of e0e_0 belong to distinct faces. Those two faces merge into one, so ff decreases by 1 and ee decreases by 1, while vv is unchanged.

The quantity v−e+fv - e + f is invariant under removing cycle edges. By induction, v−e+f=2v - e + f = 2.

▫\square
v=4,e=6,f=4⟹4−6+4=2v = 4, e = 6, f = 4 \implies 4 - 6 + 4 = 2.

Result 9 Planar Edge Bound (e≤3n−6e \le 3n - 6)

Theorem (Planar Edge Bound)

For a simple connected planar graph on n≥3n \ge 3 vertices with ee edges,

e≤3n−6.e \;\le\; 3n - 6.

Proof

Face Lengths ≥3\ge 3: Since GG is simple and n≥3n \ge 3, every face boundary has length ≥3\ge 3.

Double Counting: Summing face lengths counts each edge twice: ∑Fℓ(F)=2e≥3f⟹f≤2e3\sum_F \ell(F) = 2e \ge 3f \implies f \le \frac{2e}{3}.

Combine with Euler: Substitute f=e−n+2f = e - n + 2 into the inequality:

e−n+2≤2e3⟹3e−3n+6≤2e⟹e≤3n−6.e - n + 2 \;\le\; \frac{2e}{3} \;\implies\; 3e - 3n + 6 \;\le\; 2e \;\implies\; e \;\le\; 3n - 6.

▫\square
K5K_5: n=5,e=10>9=3n−6n = 5, e = 10 > 9 = 3n - 6 (Non-planar).

Result 10 Girth and Planar Bound

Theorem (Girth Bound)

Let GG be simple, connected, planar with nn vertices, ee edges, and girth r≥3r \ge 3. Then

e≤r(n−2)r−2.e \;\le\; \frac{r(n - 2)}{r - 2}.

Proof

Since girth is rr, every face has boundary length ≥r\ge r. Thus 2e=∑Fℓ(F)≥rf⟹f≤2er2e = \sum_F \ell(F) \ge rf \implies f \le \frac{2e}{r}.

Substituting f=e−n+2f = e - n + 2 from Euler's formula:

e−n+2≤2er⟹re−rn+2r≤2e⟹e(r−2)≤r(n−2).e - n + 2 \;\le\; \frac{2e}{r} \;\implies\; re - rn + 2r \;\le\; 2e \;\implies\; e(r - 2) \;\le\; r(n - 2).

Dividing by (r−2)(r - 2) gives e≤r(n−2)r−2e \le \frac{r(n - 2)}{r - 2}.

▫\square

Result 11 The Petersen Graph is Not Hamiltonian

Theorem (Petersen, 1898)

The Petersen graph PP has no Hamiltonian cycle: there is no cycle in PP that visits all 1010 vertices exactly once.

Proof (Structure of a Hypothetical Hamiltonian Cycle)

Setup. Write PP as two 55-cycles joined by a perfect matching of five "spokes":

A=a0a1a2a3a4a0,B=b0b2b4b1b3b0,M={aibi:i=0,…,4}.A = a_0a_1a_2a_3a_4a_0, \qquad B = b_0b_2b_4b_1b_3b_0, \qquad M = \{a_ib_i : i = 0,\dots,4\}.

The index rules for the two cycles are different, and this is the crux:

aiaj∈E(A)⇔i−j≡±1(mod5),bibj∈E(B)⇔i−j≡±2(mod5).a_ia_j \in E(A) \iff i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 5, \qquad b_ib_j \in E(B) \iff i - j \equiv \pm 2 \pmod 5.

Suppose, for contradiction, that CC is a Hamiltonian cycle of PP. The matching MM is the only connection between AA and BB, so every time CC leaves AA it must return: CC uses an even number of spokes. Since CC cannot use 00 spokes (it would be trapped in A∪BA \cup B, which is disconnected), CC uses 22 or 44 spokes.

  1. Case 1: CC uses exactly 22 spokes, say aibia_ib_i and ajbja_jb_j. Then C∩AC \cap A is a single path on all 55 vertices of AA, i.e. a Hamiltonian path of the 55-cycle AA with endpoints ai,aja_i, a_j. In a 55-cycle the endpoints of a Hamiltonian path are always adjacent, so i−j≡±1(mod5)i - j \equiv \pm 1 \pmod 5. Likewise C∩BC \cap B is a Hamiltonian path of BB with the same index endpoints bi,bjb_i, b_j, forcing i−j≡±2(mod5)i - j \equiv \pm 2 \pmod 5. Contradiction.
  2. Case 2: CC uses exactly 44 spokes. Then exactly one spoke ambma_mb_m is unused. Since ama_m has degree 22 in CC and neither of its CC-edges is in MM, both lie in AA: the vertex ama_m is internal to a path of C∩AC \cap A. Hence that path must run through both AA-neighbours of ama_m, i.e. it is am−1amam+1a_{m-1}a_ma_{m+1}, and the remaining two vertices am+2,am+3a_{m+2}, a_{m+3} form the other AA-path. By the same reasoning applied to BB (whose neighbours of bmb_m are bm±2b_{m\pm 2}), we get C∩B={bm+2bmbm−2,bm+1bm−1}.C \cap B = \{\, b_{m+2}b_mb_{m-2},\; b_{m+1}b_{m-1} \,\}. But now the endpoints am+1,am−1a_{m+1}, a_{m-1} of the first AA-path are matched to bm+1,bm−1b_{m+1}, b_{m-1} — exactly the endpoints of the second BB-path. So CC contains the closed 55-cycle am−1amam+1bm+1bm−1am−1,a_{m-1}\,a_m\,a_{m+1}\,b_{m+1}\,b_{m-1}\,a_{m-1}, This already contradicts the assumption that CC is a single cycle through all ten vertices. Every vertex on the displayed 55-cycle already has its two incident edges of CC.

Both possibilities are impossible, so PP admits no Hamiltonian cycle.

▫\square
Petersen graph: outer 55-cycle AA (blue), inner 55-cycle BB (grey), and the perfect matching MM of five spokes (orange). Any Hamiltonian cycle would need 22 or 44 spokes — both lead to a contradiction.
Remarks

The Petersen graph is a cubic non-Hamiltonian graph: 1010 vertices, 1515 edges, 33-regular, girth 55, non-planar, vertex-transitive and edge-transitive.

It is hypohamiltonian — deleting any single vertex leaves a graph that does have a Hamiltonian cycle — and it does possess a 22-factor, namely the two disjoint 55-cycles A∪BA \cup B.

Removing the 55 spokes from a Hamiltonian-cycle attempt is precisely the trap exploited above: a perfect matching whose complement is two 55-cycles rather than one 1010-cycle.

Result 11 The Petersen Graph is Not Planar

Theorem

The Petersen graph PP — 1010 vertices, 1515 edges, 33-regular, girth 55 — is not planar.

Proof 1 — Girth Bound (Edge Counting)

Step 1: the girth of PP is 55. PP is vertex-transitive and the neighbourhood of any vertex is independent — e.g. N(v0)={v1,v4,u0}N(v_0) = \{v_1, v_4, u_0\} contains no edge — so PP is triangle-free. It also has no 44-cycle: in PP, any two non-adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbour, whereas two opposite corners of a 44-cycle would share two common neighbours. Finally, the outer pentagon v0v1v2v3v4v0v_0v_1v_2v_3v_4v_0 is a cycle of length 55, so

r=girth(P)=5.r \;=\; \operatorname{girth}(P) \;=\; 5.

Step 2: the girth bound. Suppose, for contradiction, that PP were planar. Since PP is simple, connected and n=10≥3n = 10 \ge 3, Euler's formula n−e+f=2n - e + f = 2 together with 2e=∑Fℓ(F)≥rf2e = \sum_F \ell(F) \ge rf gives

f≤2er⇒e−n+2≤2er⇒e≤r(n−2)r−2.f \;\le\; \frac{2e}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e - n + 2 \;\le\; \frac{2e}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e \;\le\; \frac{r(n-2)}{r-2}.

Step 3: contradiction. Substituting r=5r = 5 and n=10n = 10:

e≤5(10−2)5−2=403=13.3¯.e \;\le\; \frac{5\,(10-2)}{5-2} \;=\; \frac{40}{3} \;=\; 13.\overline{3}.

But PP has e=15e = 15 edges, and 15>40/315 > 40/3. This contradiction shows that PP is not planar.

▫\square
The outer pentagon (red) is a cycle of length 55; PP has no 33- or 44-cycle, so girth(P)=5\operatorname{girth}(P)=5. Then e≤5(10−2)3=13.3¯<15=e(P)e \le \frac{5(10-2)}{3} = 13.\overline{3} < 15 = e(P).
Proof 2 — Kuratowski's Theorem (Topological K3,3K_{3,3})

Kuratowski's theorem. A finite graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K5K_5 and no subdivision of K3,3K_{3,3}. It therefore suffices to exhibit a subdivision of K3,3K_{3,3} inside PP.

Presentation of PP. Write

V(P)={v0,…,v4}∪{u0,…,u4},V(P) = \{v_0,\dots,v_4\} \cup \{u_0,\dots,u_4\},

with the two 55-cycles v0v1v2v3v4v0v_0v_1v_2v_3v_4v_0 and u0u2u4u1u3u0u_0u_2u_4u_1u_3u_0, joined by the five spokes vjujv_ju_j, j=0,…,4j = 0,\dots,4.

Branch vertices. Take the two independent triples

A={v1,u3,u4},B={v4,u2,u1}.A = \{v_1,\,u_3,\,u_4\}, \qquad B = \{v_4,\,u_2,\,u_1\}.

The remaining four vertices v0,v2,v3,u0v_0,\,v_2,\,v_3,\,u_0 will serve as the internal vertices of the subdivision.

The nine paths. Each vertex of AA is joined to each vertex of BB by one of the following paths:

v4v_4u2u_2u1u_1
v1v_1v1v0v4v_1 v_0 v_4v1v2u2v_1 v_2 u_2v1u1v_1 u_1
u3u_3u3v3v4u_3 v_3 v_4u3u0u2u_3 u_0 u_2u3u1u_3 u_1
u4u_4u4v4u_4 v_4u4u2u_4 u_2u4u1u_4 u_1

Every entry of the table is indeed a path in PP: the length-11 entries are edges of PP, and the four length-22 entries pass through v0v_0, v2v_2, v3v_3, u0u_0 respectively — each internal vertex occurring in exactly one path. Hence the nine paths are pairwise internally disjoint, so they form a subdivision of K3,3K_{3,3} with branch sets AA and BB.

Conclusion. PP contains a subdivision of K3,3K_{3,3}; by Kuratowski's theorem, PP is not planar. (The two edges v0u0v_0u_0 and v2v3v_2v_3 of PP are simply not used by the subdivision.)

▫\square

Remarks

The two arguments are logically independent: Proof 1 is purely analytic (Euler's formula plus the girth constraint), while Proof 2 is structural (Kuratowski's forbidden-subdivision criterion).

The same girth argument disposes of K3,3K_{3,3} itself: its girth is 44, so the bound gives e≤4(6−2)4−2=8e \le \frac{4(6-2)}{4-2} = 8, but e(K3,3)=9e(K_{3,3}) = 9.

PP is the unique (3,5)(3,5)-cage — the smallest 33-regular graph of girth 55 — and the smallest cubic graph that is not 33-edge-colourable (the smallest snark).

Counting Walks in K4K_4

Setup

Let AnA_n be the number of walks of length nn between two fixed distinct vertices uu and vv of K4K_4, and let BnB_n be the number of closed walks of length nn starting and ending at uu.

Because K4K_4 is vertex-transitive, AnA_n depends only on nn, not on the particular pair (u,v)(u,v).

Recurrences

A walk of length n+1n+1 from uu to vv must arrive at vv from a neighbour of vv — that is, from uu or from one of the two remaining vertices:

An+1=Bn+2An.A_{n+1} = B_n + 2A_n.

Likewise, a closed walk of length n+1n+1 at uu must arrive from one of the three neighbours of uu:

Bn+1=3An.B_{n+1} = 3A_n.

Eliminating BnB_n using Bn=3An−1B_n = 3A_{n-1} (valid for n≥1n \ge 1) gives

An+1=3An−1+2An,A_{n+1} = 3A_{n-1} + 2A_n,

i.e. the linear recurrence An+1−2An−3An−1=0A_{n+1} - 2A_n - 3A_{n-1} = 0.

Closed Form via the Characteristic Equation

The characteristic equation is

r2−2r−3=0,r^2 - 2r - 3 = 0,

with roots r=3r = 3 and r=−1r = -1. Therefore

An=α3n+β(−1)nA_n = \alpha\,3^n + \beta\,(-1)^n

for constants α,β\alpha, \beta.

Initial conditions: A0=0A_0 = 0 (no walk of length 00 between distinct vertices) and A1=1A_1 = 1 (the single edge uvuv). Substituting:

α+β=0,3α−β=1.\alpha + \beta = 0, \qquad 3\alpha - \beta = 1.

Solving gives α=14\alpha = \tfrac14 and β=−14\beta = -\tfrac14. Hence

An=3n−(−1)n4.A_n = \frac{3^n - (-1)^n}{4}.

For n=2,3,4,5n = 2,3,4,5 this yields 2,7,20,612, 7, 20, 61, respectively.

Result 11 Moore Graphs are Regular

Theorem (Moore Graph Regularity)

Let XX be a graph with diameter dd and girth 2d+12d+1 (such a graph is called a Moore graph). Then XX is regular — every vertex of XX has the same degree.

Proof
  1. Short paths are unique. Two distinct simple paths with the same endpoints, both of length at most dd, would contain a cycle of length at most 2d2d. The girth excludes this, so each pair has exactly one path of length at most dd by the diameter hypothesis.
  2. Vertices at distance dd have equal degree. Take u,vu,v at distance dd and let PP be their shortest path. For each neighbour xx of uu other than the first vertex after uu on PP, the unique short path from xx to vv avoids uu: going through uu would need at least d+1d+1 edges. If this path had length at most d−1d-1, prepending uxux would give a second uu–vv path of length at most dd. Its length is therefore dd. Let yy be its last vertex before vv. The resulting uu–yy path has length dd and begins with uxux. The vertex yy cannot be the neighbour of vv on PP, since the corresponding segment of PP would be a second short path from uu to yy. Distinct choices of xx give distinct choices of yy, again by uniqueness. Thus deg(u)−1≤deg(v)−1\deg(u)-1\le\deg(v)-1. Reversing uu and vv gives equality.
  3. Adjacent vertices also have equal degree. A leaf would have a neighbour from which every vertex is at distance at most d−1d-1. A shortest-path tree rooted there would give a cycle of length at most 2d−12d-1 from any edge outside the tree. Such an edge exists because the graph has a cycle, so there are no leaves. Now take any edge vuvu. Extend it to a walk of length d+1d+1 without immediately retracing an edge. The girth makes this walk a simple path. If ww is its endpoint, the uu–ww segment has length dd and is the unique short path. Also, a vv–ww path shorter than dd would combine with the constructed path to give a cycle of length at most 2d2d. Hence ww is at distance dd from both uu and vv. Step 2 gives deg(u)=deg(w)=deg(v)\deg(u)=\deg(w)=\deg(v).

Connectivity now gives the same degree at every vertex.

Remarks

Regularity is exactly what makes the Moore bound meaningful: if XX has diameter dd, girth 2d+12d+1 and every vertex has degree kk, then the shortest paths from any root are unique up to depth dd. With degree kk, they give the Moore bound (with equality here):

n=1+k+k(k−1)+k(k−1)2+⋯+k(k−1)d−1.n \;=\; 1 + k + k(k-1) + k(k-1)^2 + \cdots + k(k-1)^{d-1}.

Known Moore graphs are the complete graphs Kk+1K_{k+1} (d=1d = 1), the odd cycles C2d+1C_{2d+1} (degree 22), the Petersen graph (d=2d = 2, k=3k = 3) and the Hoffman–Singleton graph (d=2d = 2, k=7k = 7). The existence of a Moore graph with d=2d = 2 and k=57k = 57 is a famous open problem.

Enumeration All 34 Graphs on 5 Vertices & Self-Complementary Graphs

All 3434 pairwise non-isomorphic simple graphs on 55 vertices: 2121 connected (rows 11–44 plus the first graph of row 55) and 1313 disconnected (the remaining graphs).
Problem

Let X=(V,E)X = (V, E) be a self-complementary rr-regular graph. Show that r=2kr = 2k for some kk, and hence deduce that |V|=4k+1|V| = 4k + 1. Also show that the diameter of these graphs is 22.

Solution
  1. 1. Degree–order relation. If XX is rr-regular on n=|V|n = |V| vertices, its complement X¯\overline{X} is (n−1−r)(n-1-r)-regular. Since X≅X¯X \cong \overline{X}, regularity is preserved, so r=n−1−r⇒n=2r+1.r = n - 1 - r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = 2r + 1.
  2. 2. Parity of (n2)\binom{n}{2}. Self-complementarity forces |E(X)|=|E(X¯)|=12(n2)|E(X)| = |E(\overline{X})| = \tfrac{1}{2}\binom{n}{2}, so (n2)\binom{n}{2} must be even. Since n=2r+1n = 2r+1 is odd, 4∣n(n−1)4 \mid n(n-1) forces 4∣n−14 \mid n-1, i.e. n≡1(mod4).n \equiv 1 \pmod 4. Writing n=4k+1n = 4k + 1 gives r=n−12=2kr = \dfrac{n-1}{2} = 2k, as required.
  3. 3. Diameter is 22. Suppose u≁vu \not\sim v have no common neighbour. Then N(u)∩N(v)=⌀N(u) \cap N(v) = \varnothing, so |N(u)∪N(v)|=2r=4k.|N(u) \cup N(v)| = 2r = 4k. But N(u)∪N(v)⊆V\{u}N(u) \cup N(v) \subseteq V \setminus \{u\} and |V\{u}|=n−1=4k|V \setminus \{u\}| = n - 1 = 4k. Hence V\{u}=N(u)∪N(v)V \setminus \{u\} = N(u) \cup N(v), which forces v∈N(u)v \in N(u) — contradicting u≁vu \not\sim v.
    Therefore every non-adjacent pair has a common neighbour, so every pair of vertices is at distance ≤2\le 2. Since XX is self-complementary, it is not complete (for n≥2n \ge 2), so some pair is non-adjacent, giving diam(X)=2\operatorname{diam}(X) = 2.
▫\square
Remarks

Such graphs exist precisely for n≡1(mod4)n \equiv 1 \pmod 4. The smallest examples are C5C_5 (n=5n = 5, r=2r = 2) and the Paley graph of order 99 (n=9n = 9, r=4r = 4); the next are the Paley graph of order 1313 and the 1313-vertex self-complementary graphs.

The diameter-22 conclusion is characteristic of all self-complementary graphs on n≥5n \ge 5 vertices, not just the regular ones.

Result 16 The Smallest Asymmetric Tree

Theorem (Smallest Asymmetric Tree)

The smallest asymmetric tree has 77 vertices. A concrete example is the tree obtained from a central vertex cc by attaching three paths of lengths 11, 22, and 33.

Proof (Why it is asymmetric)
  1. 1. Unique degree-3 vertex. The central vertex cc is the unique vertex of degree 33. Hence every automorphism of the tree must fix cc.
  2. 2. Branches distinguished by length. The three branches attached to cc have lengths 11, 22, and 33. Since these lengths are pairwise different, each branch must be mapped onto itself by any automorphism fixing cc.
  3. 3. Only the identity survives. A path has only the identity and reflection as automorphisms, but a reflection would swap the two ends of the branch. The end of a branch adjacent to cc is not a leaf (for branches of length ≥2\ge 2), so such a reflection cannot fix cc. Therefore only the identity automorphism exists, and the tree is asymmetric.
▫\square
Remarks

Every tree on at most 66 vertices admits a nontrivial automorphism; the example above shows the bound 77 is attained.

For comparison, the smallest asymmetric graph (not necessarily a tree) has only 66 vertices — trees are more rigid in this sense, and 77 is exactly the smallest order of an asymmetric tree.

The unique degree-33 vertex cc (red) is fixed by every automorphism. The three branches have pairwise distinct lengths 11, 22, 33 (blue), so each branch is preserved — leaving only the identity automorphism.

Classification Trees on 7 Vertices — Degree Sequences

Examples

Four trees on 77 vertices, distinguished by their degree sequences:

(6,16),(5,2,15),(4,3,15),(4,2,2,14).(6,1^6), \qquad (5,2,1^5), \qquad (4,3,1^5), \qquad (4,2,2,1^4).

Here 1m1^m denotes mm leaves. All four are pairwise non-isomorphic, since no two share the same degree sequence.

(6,16)(6,1^6) — star with a degree-66 hub.
(5,2,15)(5,2,1^5) — one branch extended to length 22.
(4,3,15)(4,3,1^5) — a degree-44 centre with one degree-33 branch vertex (orange).
(4,2,2,14)(4,2,2,1^4) — two degree-22 branch vertices (orange), two pendant leaves.
Remarks

These four trees are among the 1111 pairwise non-isomorphic trees on 77 vertices. They illustrate the range of degree sequences: K1,6K_{1,6} has the largest possible degree, while (4,2,2,14)(4,2,2,1^4) has the largest number of degree-22 vertices.

The asymmetric tree of the previous slide — a centre with pendant paths of lengths 1,2,31,2,3 — has degree sequence (3,2,2,2,1,1,1)(3,2,2,2,1,1,1), which is not among the four above. Its three branch lengths being pairwise distinct is precisely what kills all nontrivial automorphisms.

In general, the degree sequence of a tree determines neither its isomorphism class nor its symmetry: here, the same collection of degrees can arise from structurally different trees.

Havel–Hakimi Algorithm & Graphical Sequences

Slide 18
1  ·  Basic Definitions
Definition 1 · Degree Sequence

A degree sequence of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with |V|=n|V|=n is the multiset

(deg(v1),deg(v2),…,deg(vn)),(\deg(v_1),\ \deg(v_2),\ \dots,\ \deg(v_n)),

usually written in non-increasing order: d1≥d2≥…≥dn≥0d_1\ge d_2\ge\dots\ge d_n\ge 0.

Definition 2 · Graphical Sequence

A sequence d=(d1,…,dn)d=(d_1,\dots,d_n) of non-negative integers is graphical if there exists a simple graph (no loops, no multiple edges) with nn vertices whose degrees are exactly d1,d2,…,dnd_1,d_2,\dots,d_n.

Handshaking Lemma

If d=(d1,…,dn)d=(d_1,\dots,d_n) is graphical then ∑i=1ndi\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_i is even.

Necessary but Not Sufficient

An even sum is necessary but not sufficient. For example (1,1,1)(1,1,1) fails immediately (odd sum). But (3,3,3)(3,3,3) also fails: its sum is 99 (odd), yet a simple graph on 33 vertices cannot have degree 33 (maximum degree is 22). The Havel–Hakimi algorithm resolves all such cases systematically.

2  ·  The Havel–Hakimi Algorithm
Algorithm (Havel–Hakimi)

Given d=(d1,d2,…,dn)d=(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n) with d1≥d2≥…≥dn≥0d_1\ge d_2\ge\dots\ge d_n\ge 0:

  1. If all entries are 00, stop: graphical.
  2. If some entry is negative, or d1>n−1d_1>n-1, stop: not graphical.
  3. Remove d1d_1 and subtract 11 from each of the next d1d_1 entries, i.e. set di↦di−1d_i \mapsto d_i-1 for i=2,…,d1+1i=2,\dots,d_1+1.
  4. Reorder the remaining n−1n-1 entries in non-increasing order.
  5. Repeat on the new sequence.
Theorem (Havel–Hakimi, 1955)

A non-increasing sequence d=(d1,…,dn)d=(d_1,\dots,d_n) of non-negative integers is graphical if and only if the reduced sequence

d′=(d2−1,d3−1,…,dd1+1−1,dd1+2,…,dn)d'=(d_2-1,\ d_3-1,\ \dots,\ d_{d_1+1}-1,\ d_{d_1+2},\ \dots,\ d_n)

(reordered non-increasing) is graphical.

Key Idea

Attach the highest-degree vertex v1v_1 to the d1d_1 next-highest-degree vertices. If any simple graph realises dd, then some such graph does so with v1v_1 adjacent to precisely those d1d_1 vertices. So we may assume this without loss of generality and recurse.

3  ·  Illustrated Example 1 — a Graphical Sequence
Example 1 · (3,3,2,2,2)(3,3,2,2,2)

Initial: (3,3,2,2,2)(3,3,2,2,2), n=5n=5.

Step 1. Remove d1=3d_1=3; subtract 11 from the next 33 entries:

(3,3_,2_,2_,2)→(2,1,1,2).(3,\ \underline{3},\ \underline{2},\ \underline{2},\ 2) \longrightarrow (2,\ 1,\ 1,\ 2).

Reorder: (2,2,1,1)(2,2,1,1).

Step 2. Remove d1=2d_1=2; subtract 11 from the next 22 entries:

(2,2_,1_,1)→(1,0,1).(2,\ \underline{2},\ \underline{1},\ 1) \longrightarrow (1,\ 0,\ 1).

Reorder: (1,1,0)(1,1,0).

Step 3. Remove d1=1d_1=1; subtract 11 from the next 11 entry:

(1,1_,0)→(0,0).(1,\ \underline{1},\ 0) \longrightarrow (0,\ 0).

Reorder: (0,0)(0,0).

Step 4. All zeros ⇒\Rightarrow graphical.

Realisation of (3,3,2,2,2)(3,3,2,2,2): degrees A=3A=3, B=3B=3, C=2C=2, D=2D=2, E=2E=2.
4  ·  Illustrated Example 2 — a Non-Graphical Sequence
Example 2 · (5,5,5,1,1,1)(5,5,5,1,1,1)

Initial: (5,5,5,1,1,1)(5,5,5,1,1,1), n=6n=6. Sum =18=18 (even, so parity does not rule it out).

Step 1. Remove d1=5d_1=5; subtract 11 from the next 55 entries:

(5,5_,5_,1_,1_,1_)→(4,4,0,0,0).(5,\ \underline{5},\ \underline{5},\ \underline{1},\ \underline{1},\ \underline{1}) \longrightarrow (4,\ 4,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0).

Reorder: (4,4,0,0,0)(4,4,0,0,0).

Step 2. Remove d1=4d_1=4; subtract 11 from the next 44 entries:

(4,4_,0_,0_,0_)→(3,−1,−1,−1).(4,\ \underline{4},\ \underline{0},\ \underline{0},\ \underline{0}) \longrightarrow (3,\ -1,\ -1,\ -1).

A negative entry appears ⇒\Rightarrow not graphical.

Why It Fails Structurally

Each of the three degree-55 vertices would have to be adjacent to every other vertex. Then each degree-11 vertex would be adjacent to all three degree-55 vertices, forcing degree ≥3\ge 3. Contradiction.

6  ·  Pseudocode
Havel–Hakimi Pseudocode 
function isGraphical(d):
    d = sort(d, descending)
    while d is not all zeros:
        if d[0] < 0 or d[0] >= len(d):
            return False
        k = d[0]
        d = d[1:]                 # drop the first element
        for i in range(k):
            d[i] = d[i] - 1
        if any(x < 0 for x in d):
            return False
        d = sort(d, descending)
    return True
Complexity

At most nn iterations, each with a sort costing O(nlogn)O(n\log n).

Total: O(n2logn)O(n^2 \log n).

7  ·  Practice Problems
Exercise Set

Decide whether each sequence is graphical. If yes, sketch a realisation.

  1. (4,4,3,3,3,3)(4,4,3,3,3,3)
  2. (3,3,3,3,2,2)(3,3,3,3,2,2)
  3. (6,6,5,5,4,4,4,3,3)(6,6,5,5,4,4,4,3,3)
  4. (2,2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2,2)
  5. (5,4,3,2,1,0)(5,4,3,2,1,0)
Answers
  1. Yes. Two degree-44 vertices A,BA,B; four degree-33 vertices C,D,E,FC,D,E,F. Edges: AA–B,C,D,EB,C,D,E and BB–C,D,E,FC,D,E,F and FF–C,D,EC,D,E.
  2. Yes. The triangular prism.
  3. Yes. (Use Havel–Hakimi; it reduces to zeros.)
  4. Yes. C6C_6.
  5. No. The degree-55 vertex must be adjacent to all others, but the degree-00 vertex cannot be adjacent to anyone.
8  ·  Key Takeaways
Remember
  1. The sum of the degrees must be even (Handshaking Lemma).
  2. Every entry must satisfy 0≤di≤n−10 \le d_i \le n-1.
  3. Havel–Hakimi: remove the largest entry, subtract 11 from the next-largest entries, re-sort, and repeat.
  4. A negative entry at any stage ⇒\Rightarrow not graphical.
  5. All zeros reached ⇒\Rightarrow graphical.
  6. The algorithm implicitly constructs a realisation: the removed vertex is adjacent to exactly the vertices whose degrees were decremented.
